title: What counts as conversion practice: survivors, law and religion
label: 2 November 2026 · Draft Conversion Practices Bill evidence session
summary: Survivors Deputy Jayne Ozanne and Ian Smith told the Joint Committee why a law banning conversion practices matters, criticised the draft Bill’s narrow legal tests, and urged clearer rules that focus on the purpose of the abuser, the harms of suppression and better training and routes to protect victims — especially children — rather than relying on high criminal thresholds that will rarely be met.

speakers.label: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
speakers.name: Deputy Jayne Ozanne OBE
speakers.role: Parliamentarian in Guernsey; campaigner who led the Ban Conversion Therapy coalition

speakers.label: Ian Smith
speakers.name: Ian Smith
speakers.role: Survivor of conversion practices and respondent to the Government consultation

glossary.definition: A broad label for actions aimed at changing, suppressing or 'healing' someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
Telling someone they must hide or not act on their sexuality or gender identity, for example insisting on celibacy.
When the person providing help aims from the start to change or make someone not be LGBT+, rather than support them.
Crown Prosecution Service, which decides whether to bring criminal charges in England and Wales.
Therapeutic approach that supports a person's stated gender identity or sexuality rather than trying to change it.
A legal advisory report (chaired by Baroness Helena Kennedy) proposing a definition and structure for banning conversion practices.

chapters.title: Why this law matters
chapters.takeaway: Survivors say the law signals society's rejection of conversion practices and could deter institutions that ran or enabled abuse.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We're examining the draft Conversion Practices Bill; thank you both for coming. Could you outline your overall view on banning abusive conversion practices?

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: I'm glad there's a Bill after years of delay. Conversion practices are an umbrella term — not everyone recognises it — and many people, including me, have suffered for years from prayer, exorcisms and religious counselling.

turns.speaker: Ian Smith
turns.text: I'm here as someone who suffered these practices. Institutions that oversaw my 'help' never seemed to think anything was wrong. A law would have mattered to me because it signals the country takes victims' liberty seriously.

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: The delay emboldened perpetrators. We need the law — but it must define practices properly and protect people early, not only after serious harm.

chapters.title: What survivors experienced
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses describe long-term, often religiously framed attempts to change them that caused shame, mental distress and suicidal thoughts.

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: I spent 20 years seeking prayer, exorcisms and psychotherapies to 'fix' me. It was loving on the surface but mentally torturous; I ended up in hospital after years of shame and self-denial.

turns.speaker: Ian Smith
turns.text: I consented to exorcisms and prayer, and later therapy; it took a Netflix documentary and a psychiatrist telling me 'there's nothing wrong with being gay' before I recognised I was a victim.

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: Most victims we surveyed were young: over half under 18 and three-quarters under 24. The common pattern is secrecy, pressure from family or religious leaders, and escalating interventions.

turns.speaker: Ian Smith
turns.text: Young brains are still developing; having groups of peers or church leaders praying over you can be especially damaging and controlling.

chapters.title: Problems with the Bill's drafting
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses argue the Bill focuses too much on victims proving serious harm and not enough on the abuser's intent or suppression.

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: I think the Bill focuses wrongly on causation and on the victim's harm. Other jurisdictions focus on the practitioner's purpose — the 'predetermined purpose' to change or suppress — which is clearer and safer.

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: Calling some forms 'non-abusive' gives a licence for prayer or counselling to continue. The 'serious harm' threshold is too high and shifts the burden onto victims.

turns.speaker: Ian Smith
turns.text: Legally I can't analyse every threshold, but practically a law that says 'this behaviour is unacceptable' would have helped. Institutions should be warned that these practices are not okay.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: If the Bill had been law when you suffered, would it have helped?

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: It would have signalled a bar to society and helped in prosecuting institutional courses of conduct, though I doubt it would cover everyday prayer as drafted.

chapters.title: Religion, prayer and the line to criminality
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses say holding religious beliefs is protected, but practices aimed at changing someone cause harm and must be addressed; one-off prayers should be treated differently from purposeful attempts to change someone.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: How do we balance freedom of religion with stopping harm — should the law cover the first prayer or only sustained interventions?

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: Holding a belief is protected. The issue is practice. A one-off prayer for peace is different from praying to make someone 'straight.' That difference is the 'predetermined purpose.'

turns.speaker: Ian Smith
turns.text: Practices that call on a higher power to make a change for someone else are the ones that felt most coercive to me.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Do you think the Bill as drafted would criminalise parents or single religious leaders?

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: We should be clear that any conversion practice is wrong. But the Bill as drafted sets thresholds so high that parents or single leaders are unlikely to be prosecuted; the law should still say it's prohibited.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: Could the law produce a chilling effect on genuine pastoral or counselling conversations?

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: Exploratory, supportive conversations are acceptable. The problem is when the helper's mind is made up and they channel someone towards a single outcome — that's coercive.

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: Drafting is difficult, which is why we should follow other jurisdictions that focused on intent and suppression.

chapters.title: Evidence, prosecution and children
chapters.takeaway: High prosecutorial thresholds and survivors' shame and fear make evidence collection hard; witnesses support risk-based rules for children and better training for police and services.

turns.speaker: Lord Hope of Craighead
turns.text: Prosecutors need evidence of the practice, harm and intent. Victims face barriers — how can the law work in practice?

turns.speaker: Ian Smith
turns.text: Victims distrust authorities and often lack documentary evidence. Institutions' records and multiple witnesses can help, but many victims just won't come forward.

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: Shame, family ties and fear of losing relationships stop people testifying. Waiting until someone is hospitalised is too late; removing the 'serious harm' bar or using a 'risk' test for children helps.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: Why haven't police acted more in the past?

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: There has been a lack of training and tools. We need an education package for police, social workers, NHS staff and teachers to spot and respond to conversion practices.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: How do we handle borderline situations, like a child blocked from getting a binder — could that be abuse under the Bill?

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: Context matters: is it one-off, a parent's religious belief, or a sustained course of conduct? We need reasonableness defences and to include children because most victims are young.

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: De-transitioning and fluid identities complicate things, but the focus must be protecting people from clearly harmful practices while allowing proper therapeutic help.

chapters.title: Practical suggestions and final points
chapters.takeaway: Survivors ask the Committee to focus the law on the abuser's intent to change or suppress, lower criminal thresholds for children or use 'risk', add civil protection orders and invest in training.

turns.speaker: Deputy Jayne Ozanne
turns.text: Follow other countries: define conversion practices to include intent to change or suppress, consider civil protection orders alongside criminal offences, and include overseas provisions.

turns.speaker: Ian Smith
turns.text: Even if prosecutions are rare, the law's preventive message matters. Hold institutions to account and give victims routes to be heard without destroying family relationships.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. You've been candid and helpful. You may follow up in writing if you wish; the Committee is grateful for your evidence today.
